source: CARDI (Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute) technical bulletin, "Selecting Soil Groups for Rice Cultivation" (ការធ្វើចំណាត់ថ្នាក់ដីសម្រាប់ដំណាំស្រូវ), published February 2006, authored by Chan Phaloeun, CARDI, funded by the Cambodia-Australia Agricultural Extension Project (CAAEP/AusAID)
text:
Cambodia's rice soils are grouped into a national soil classification system (10 major soil groups referenced in this bulletin, e.g. Prey Khmer, Prateah Lang, Labansiek, Krakor, Bakan, Kbal Po Pil, Koun Svay, Tuol Samraong, Koktrob, Kampong Siem) so that extension workers and farmers can match the right variety and fertilizer recommendation to the soil actually present in a given field. Rather than relying only on laboratory testing, CARDI developed a simple field diagnostic method — a step-by-step yes/no question key — that an extension worker or trained farmer can walk through directly in the field using a few basic tools.

Why soil classification matters for rice: different soil groups differ in texture, structure, color, hardpan depth, and drainage, all of which affect nutrient availability and water-holding capacity — and therefore affect which variety and fertilizer approach will perform well.

Field properties used to identify a soil group: the key asks about a sequence of physically observable soil traits, checked in this general order:
1. Topsoil texture (sandy vs. clay vs. loam) — checked by feel: rubbing moistened soil between the fingers.
2. Topsoil color and whether topsoil and subsoil colors are clearly different from each other.
3. Depth to a mottled zone (rust/grey mottling, an indicator of seasonal waterlogging) — commonly checked at thresholds around 20 cm, 30-40 cm, and 50 cm deep.
4. Whether a hardpan (compacted or plinthic layer) is present, and how deep it sits.
5. Presence of lime nodules, gypsum crystals, or visible salt crusts in the profile.
6. Soil pH, checked with a simple field pH meter or pH test kit.
7. Estimated organic matter/fertility level, sometimes cross-checked against expected paddy yield (e.g. below vs. above roughly 1.2 tonnes/hectare as a rough fertility indicator in the key).

How the diagnostic key works: starting from the topsoil texture question, the user answers "yes" (ada) or "no" (te) to each question in turn; each answer branches to either another question or to a final soil-group identification (e.g. reaching "Prateah Lang, brown-color subgroup" or "Bakan group"). The key is organized as three separate branching keys depending on the general landscape position of the field: a key for higher/upland rice land, a key for medium (mid-toposequence) rice land, and a key for low-lying/deepwater rainfed rice land — since soil development differs by position on the landscape relative to drainage.

Basic equipment needed for field diagnosis: a soil auger or spade to dig a shallow profile pit, a ruler or tape measure to record mottle/hardpan depth, a Munsell-style color chart (or careful visual comparison) for topsoil and subsoil color, a field pH meter or pH test kit, and a notebook to record the yes/no answers so the final soil-group call can be cross-checked later.

How this connects to fertilizer and variety decisions: once a field's soil group is identified using this key, that identification links back to the 11 CARDI soil-group profiles (with their associated NPK fertilizer guidance) already in the knowledge base — this diagnostic method is the field-level "how do I find out which group my field is" step that precedes applying those group-specific fertilizer rates.
caveat: This entry documents the field diagnostic KEY/methodology itself (the sequence of yes/no soil-property questions used to identify a soil group), not the full set of soil-group profiles with their specific fertilizer rates — those are already covered by the existing 11-CARDI-soil-group KB entries from an earlier batch. The source document's flowchart/decision-tree pages (the actual branching key with soil-group endpoints) are formatted as diagrams rather than clean running text, so the precise sequence and wording of every branch point could not be extracted with full confidence from the raw PDF text; this entry summarizes the general structure and the field properties used, rather than reproducing the exact branching logic question-by-question. The source counts 10 soil groups in its introduction while a related CARDI/MAFF fertilizer publication used elsewhere in this knowledge base references 11 CARDI soil groups nationally — this discrepancy is noted rather than resolved, since it isn't clear from this document alone whether it is a subset, an earlier/later revision, or a different grouping scheme. Treat the specific depth thresholds (20cm, 30-40cm, 50cm) and the 1.2 tonnes/hectare fertility cutoff as illustrative examples of the kind of threshold used, not as universally exact values for every soil group.
